sun.name: The Sun
sun.introduction: is our home star: a 4.6-billion-year-old yellow dwarf that holds about 99.86% of the Solar System’s mass. Its light reaches Earth in about eight minutes and powers our climate and almost all life.

sections.title: Brighter than most of its neighbors
sections.text: The Sun is often called an ordinary star, yet it outshines about 85% of the stars in the Milky Way, most of which are dim red dwarfs. Its neighborhood follows the same pattern: within 11 light-years, only Sirius A and Alpha Centauri A give off more light. Because it is the star we know best, astronomers measure other stars’ masses, radii and luminosities in solar units.

sections.title: A furnace with a hotter crown
sections.text: In the core, at about 15 million °C, hydrogen fuses into helium. The visible surface is a comparatively mild 5,500 °C, yet the thin outer atmosphere, the corona, reaches up to about 2 million °C. Why the corona is so much hotter than the surface below it is one of the long-standing puzzles of solar physics.

source.title: NASA: Sun facts

sections.title: An 11-year heartbeat
sections.text: Roughly every 11 years the Sun’s magnetic poles swap places, and its activity swings from calm to stormy and back. Near maximum, twisted magnetic fields produce sunspots, flares and eruptions that can disturb satellites and power grids and paint auroras across Earth’s skies. The current cycle, Solar Cycle 25, began in December 2019.

source.title: NASA: Sun facts

sections.title: Touching the Sun
sections.text: On December 24, 2024, NASA’s Parker Solar Probe passed about 6.2 million km above the solar surface, deep inside the corona. Moving at about 690,000 km/h, it briefly became the fastest object ever built. Its repeated dives sample the region where the solar wind is accelerated.

source.title: Wikipedia: Parker Solar Probe

sections.title: A bubble, a galactic orbit and a quiet ending
sections.text: The solar wind inflates a vast bubble, the heliosphere; Voyager 1 crossed its edge in 2012, about 122 AU from the Sun. The Sun itself circles the Milky Way’s center roughly once every 230 million years. In about five billion years it will swell into a red giant, possibly engulfing Earth, then shed its outer layers and fade as a white dwarf. It is not massive enough to explode as a supernova.

alpha-centauri.name: Alpha Centauri
alpha-centauri.introduction: is the nearest star system to the Sun and the third-brightest point of light in the night sky. Its three members are the Sun-like Alpha Centauri A, the cooler orange dwarf B and the faint red dwarf Proxima Centauri, which at 4.24 light-years is the closest known star to the Sun.

sections.title: Two suns in one point of light
sections.text: To the unaided eye, A and B merge into a single star of magnitude −0.27, outshone only by Sirius and Canopus. The pair orbit each other every 80 years, their separation swinging between about 11 and 36 AU, roughly the distances of Saturn and Pluto from the Sun. A is slightly more massive and brighter than the Sun; B is a little smaller and cooler. Since 2016 and 2018, the IAU names Rigil Kentaurus and Toliman have referred to A and B.

sections.title: Proxima, the distant third
sections.text: Proxima lies much farther from A and B than they are from each other, yet it is gravitationally bound to the pair, on an orbit estimated to take about 550,000 years. It is a true member of the family rather than a chance neighbor passing by.

source.title: ESO: Proxima is bound to Alpha Centauri

sections.title: A flare star with the nearest planets
sections.text: Robert Innes discovered Proxima in 1915. At magnitude 11 it needs a telescope, yet it is a fierce flare star: in 2016 one superflare raised its visible brightness about 68-fold, almost to the limit of naked-eye visibility. Proxima b, announced in 2016, orbits every 11.2 days in the zone where liquid water could exist, given a suitable atmosphere. Proxima d, confirmed in 2025, has about a quarter of Earth’s mass and a 5.1-day year; a third signal, Proxima c, is disputed.

source.title: Wikipedia: Proxima Centauri

sections.title: A giant around A?
sections.text: Webb images taken in August 2024 revealed a faint source about twice Earth’s distance from A, possibly a gas giant with roughly Saturn’s mass. It was not seen again in February and April 2025, so it is still a candidate. If confirmed, it would be the closest planet to Earth in the habitable zone of a Sun-like star, and the closest to its star of any directly imaged planet.

source.title: ESA: Webb finds new hints for a planet around Alpha Centauri A

sections.title: The first interstellar destination
sections.text: As our nearest neighbor, Alpha Centauri is the natural first goal for interstellar travel. Breakthrough Starshot, announced in 2016, proposed launching gram-scale probes on laser-driven light sails at 15–20% of the speed of light to fly past Proxima b within 20–30 years. The project was paused in 2025.

source.title: Wikipedia: Breakthrough Starshot

sections.title: Our Sun, seen from next door
sections.text: From Alpha Centauri, the Sun would appear as a magnitude +0.5 star in eastern Cassiopeia, outshining every other star in that constellation. The system is drifting closer and should pass about 2.9 light-years from the Sun around 27,000 CE. South of about 29° S it never sets, and together with Beta Centauri it points the way to the Southern Cross.

barnards-star.name: Barnard’s Star
barnards-star.introduction: is a faint red dwarf about six light-years away in Ophiuchus, the closest single star to the Sun. No star moves faster across our sky, and it is heading toward us: around 11,800 CE it will be about 3.75 light-years away, closer than Proxima Centauri is today.

sections.title: The sky’s fastest-moving star
sections.text: Its apparent motion of about 10.3 arcseconds per year is larger than that of any other star. Over a human lifetime it shifts by a quarter of a degree, roughly half the width of the full Moon. Edward Emerson Barnard measured this motion in 1916. Spectra show it approaching at about 110 km/s.

sections.title: Older than the Sun
sections.text: At an estimated 7–12 billion years, Barnard’s Star is much older than the Sun. It turns slowly, once in about four months, and is generally calm, although astronomers caught it flaring in 1998. Old, quiet red dwarfs like this are benchmarks for how small stars age.

sections.title: Planets that were not there
sections.text: From the early 1960s, Peter van de Kamp argued that giant planets tugged on Barnard’s Star; his claims were refuted in the 1970s. The British Interplanetary Society’s Project Daedalus study still chose it as the target for an uncrewed fusion-powered probe, partly because of those planets. A 233-day super-Earth announced in 2018 was later attributed to stellar activity.

sections.title: Four tiny worlds
sections.text: ESPRESSO measurements published in 2024 revealed a small planet with a 3.15-day orbit. In 2025, an independent MAROON-X study confirmed it along with three siblings, whose minimum masses are only a fifth to a third of Earth’s. Their years last about 2.3, 3.2, 4.1 and 6.7 days, and they orbit far closer than the habitable zone. The same data rule out planets above about 0.57 Earth masses in the habitable zone itself.

source.title: Basant et al. 2025: Four sub-Earth planets orbiting Barnard’s Star

luhman-16.name: Luhman 16
luhman-16.introduction: is a pair of brown dwarfs about 6.5 light-years away in Vela, the third-closest system to the Sun after Alpha Centauri and Barnard’s Star. Too light to sustain the hydrogen fusion that powers ordinary stars, these are the nearest known brown dwarfs.

sections.title: Hidden in a crowded sky
sections.text: Kevin Luhman spotted the pair in WISE infrared data in 2013, making it the closest system found since Barnard’s Star’s motion was measured in 1916. It escaped earlier searches because it lies close to the plane of the Milky Way, where countless background stars make faint objects hard to pick out.

sections.title: The first brown-dwarf weather map
sections.text: The pair straddles the transition between L and T spectral classes, where clouds break up and methane appears. In 2014, astronomers followed how B’s spectrum changed as it rotated and assembled the first map of a brown dwarf’s surface: a large dark region at middle latitudes and a bright area near one pole, likely patchy clouds.

source.title: ESO: First weather map of a brown dwarf

sections.title: Winds in stripes
sections.text: TESS observations analyzed in 2021 suggested that high-speed winds form bands parallel to the equators, much like Jupiter’s. In 2024, Webb monitored both brown dwarfs and detected water vapor, carbon monoxide and methane, tracking how their atmospheres change as they spin.

sections.title: Weighing failed stars
sections.text: A and B orbit each other in about 27 years. Following that orbit gives masses of about 35 and 29 times Jupiter’s, measured directly rather than inferred from atmosphere models. A 2013 hint of a third body would have been the first planet found by astrometry, but Hubble follow-up made it highly unlikely.

wise-0855-0714.name: WISE 0855-0714
wise-0855-0714.introduction: is the coldest brown dwarf known: a free-floating world about 7.4 light-years away in Hydra and the fourth-closest system to the Sun. Its temperature, around 280 K, is close to the freezing point of water, more like a cold day on Earth than a stellar surface.

sections.title: Star, planet or something between?
sections.text: With an estimated 3 to 10 times Jupiter’s mass, it resembles a giant planet but has no host star. Webb’s detection of deuterated methane shows that it is below the mass needed to burn even deuterium, so it never shone by fusion at all. It is practically invisible in visible light; almost all of its glow is infrared.

sections.title: Found by its motion
sections.text: Kevin Luhman noticed its unusually large motion in 2013 while searching WISE images for distant companions of the Sun, and announced it the following year. Webb later tracked it against background objects between 2022 and 2023.

sections.title: A chemistry lab near 0 °C
sections.text: Webb spectra reveal water vapor, methane, ammonia and carbon monoxide, and a 2024 study reported about one part per billion of phosphine. Its nitrogen isotopes resemble today’s interstellar gas more than the Sun’s, a possible hint that it formed relatively recently.

sections.title: Patchy water clouds
sections.text: A September 2026 Webb study reported evidence for patchy water clouds, together with changes in carbon monoxide and phosphine absorption as the object rotates. The cloud interpretation comes from comparisons with atmospheric models.

source.title: Miles et al. 2026: Water cloud and chemical modulations

wolf-359.name: Wolf 359
wolf-359.introduction: is a very faint red dwarf about 7.9 light-years away in Leo. Only Alpha Centauri, Barnard’s Star and two brown-dwarf systems are closer. It was the faintest and least massive star known until 1944.

sections.title: Just massive enough to shine
sections.text: At about 11% of the Sun’s mass, Wolf 359 is just above the limit for sustained hydrogen fusion. Placed where the Sun is, it would look only about ten times as bright as the full Moon. Max Wolf measured its large motion on photographs in 1917; the name is its number in his 1919 catalog.

sections.title: Storms on a tiny star
sections.text: Its surface magnetic field is hundreds of times stronger than the Sun’s and powers frequent flares; Hubble once recorded 32 flares in two hours. Wolf 359 was the first star other than the Sun whose coronal spectrum was observed. It is young, probably less than a billion years old.

sections.title: A famous name in science fiction
sections.text: Wolf 359 is the site of the Battle of Wolf 359 in Star Trek, the title of an episode of the original The Outer Limits, and the setting of the Wolf 359 podcast, whose story takes place on a space station orbiting the star.

sections.title: One candidate left
sections.text: Two planet candidates were proposed in 2019. The inner signal, Wolf 359 c, turned out to come from the star’s rotation. A 2023 study could neither confirm nor rule out the outer candidate, Wolf 359 b, while excluding massive companions on a range of orbits.

source.title: Carter et al. 2023: Hunting for substellar companions around Wolf 359

lalande-21185.name: Lalande 21185
lalande-21185.introduction: is the brightest red dwarf in the northern sky, about 8.3 light-years away in Ursa Major. Also called Gliese 411, it shines at magnitude 7.5: too faint for the unaided eye, but easy to find with binoculars.

sections.title: A long paper trail
sections.text: Jérôme Lalande published its position in his star catalog in 1801. In 1857, Friedrich Argelander noticed its large proper motion, a sign of a near neighbor. It is still approaching and should pass about 4.65 light-years from the Sun in about 19,900 years.

sections.title: Planets claimed and lost
sections.text: In 1951, Peter van de Kamp claimed an astrometric detection of planets on photographic plates. In 1996, George Gatewood announced multiple planets, also from astrometry, and the news drew wide attention. Neither claim was confirmed, and Gatewood’s is now in doubt.

sections.title: Planets found at last
sections.text: Precise Doppler measurements eventually found real planets, far less massive than the giants once claimed. Gliese 411 b, confirmed in 2020, circles the star in about 12.9 days. Gliese 411 c, confirmed in 2021, has at least 14 Earth masses and an eight-year orbit. A third signal near 215 days, Gliese 411 d, is still unconfirmed.

sirius.name: Sirius
sirius.introduction: is the brightest star in Earth’s night sky, almost twice as bright as the runner-up, Canopus. It lies about 8.6 light-years away in Canis Major. The dazzling white Sirius A has a faint companion, Sirius B, the brightest and nearest white dwarf known.

sections.title: Bright because it is near
sections.text: Sirius A has about twice the Sun’s mass and gives off about 25 times as much light, but much of its brilliance comes from being one of our closest neighbors. It is slowly approaching and will brighten slightly over the next 60,000 years, to a peak magnitude of −1.68.

sections.title: The Dog Star
sections.text: Its prominence in Canis Major earned Sirius the nickname Dog Star. The ancient Greeks linked the hot “dog days” of summer to its rising. In ancient Egypt, its first appearance in the dawn sky after months of absence marked the coming flood of the Nile, and it was worshipped as the goddess Sopdet.

sections.title: A red Sirius?
sections.text: Ptolemy described Sirius as reddish, a puzzle given its pure white color today. Chinese sources consistently describe it as white, and atmospheric reddening near the horizon is one proposed explanation. The same atmosphere makes Sirius flash with color as it twinkles low in the sky.

sections.title: The companion predicted before it was seen
sections.text: In 1844, Friedrich Bessel inferred an unseen companion from a wobble in Sirius’s motion. Alvan Graham Clark first saw it in 1862 while testing an 18.5-inch refractor for the Dearborn Observatory. In 1915, Walter Adams found that Sirius B is hot and white despite being faint, so it had to be tiny and extraordinarily dense: one of the discoveries that revealed white dwarfs.

sections.title: A Sun’s mass in an Earth-sized star
sections.text: The pair orbit every 50.1 years, between about 8 and 32 AU apart. Hubble measurements give masses of 2.06 Suns for A and 1.02 for B, which is packed into a body about Earth’s size. The system is only about 230 million years old. B was once the more massive star, ran through its life faster and shed its outer layers; A will eventually follow the same path.

source.title: Bond et al. 2017: The Sirius system and its dynamical masses

luyten-726-8.name: Luyten 726-8
luyten-726-8.introduction: is a pair of small red dwarfs about 8.8 light-years away in Cetus. Its fainter member, UV Ceti, gave its name to the whole class of flaring red dwarfs. In about 31,500 years, the pair will pass within about 0.93 light-years of Epsilon Eridani.

sections.title: The original flare star
sections.text: Willem Luyten discovered the pair in 1948 from its large motion across the sky. In 1952, UV Ceti brightened 75-fold in only 20 seconds, and flare stars became known as UV Ceti variables. Its partner, BL Ceti, flares too. Both stars spin in under six hours, fast rotation that feeds their strong magnetic activity.

sections.title: Near-twins with different tempers
sections.text: The two stars orbit each other every 26.4 years along an elongated path that interferometers can follow precisely. They have almost identical masses, about 12% of the Sun’s, yet differ in their magnetic behavior, which makes them a natural experiment in how small stars generate magnetic fields.

source.title: GRAVITY Collaboration 2024: Astrometry of GJ 65

sections.title: A Neptune-class candidate
sections.text: The same GRAVITY measurements revealed a possible planet with a 156-day orbit and a mass of a few tens of Earth masses. It is unconfirmed, and it is not yet known whether it circles A or B.

source.title: GRAVITY Collaboration 2024: Neptune-mass candidate in GJ 65

ross-154.name: Ross 154
ross-154.introduction: is a red dwarf about 9.7 light-years away and the nearest star in Sagittarius. Also known as V1216 Sagittarii, it is a young, restless flare star, probably less than a billion years old.

sections.title: Fast spin, fierce flares
sections.text: Ross 154 rotates in about 2.8 days, far faster than the Sun, and its strong magnetic activity makes it a prolific flare star. During a flare it typically brightens by 3–4 magnitudes, and the Chandra X-ray Observatory has recorded powerful X-ray flares from its hot outer atmosphere.

sections.title: Found among the variables
sections.text: Frank Elmore Ross catalogued it in 1925 in a list of new variable stars. It is approaching very slowly and should pass about 6.4 light-years from the Sun in about 157,000 years.

ross-248.name: Ross 248
ross-248.introduction: is a faint red dwarf about 10.3 light-years away in Andromeda, and a future nearest star: in about 36,500 years it will pass about 3 light-years from the Sun. It is also known as Gliese 905 and HH Andromedae.

sections.title: Our next nearest neighbor
sections.text: Around its closest approach, Ross 248 should overtake Alpha Centauri as the Sun’s nearest stellar neighbor and hold that title for roughly 9,000 years. Frank Elmore Ross catalogued it in 1926 in his second list of stars with measurable proper motion.

sections.title: The first starspots beyond the Sun
sections.text: In 1950, Ross 248 became the first star whose small brightness changes were attributed to spots on its surface, rotating in and out of view. It also shows a longer brightness cycle of about 4.2 years.

sections.title: Voyager 2’s distant flyby
sections.text: In about 40,000 years, Voyager 2 will drift within about 1.7 light-years of Ross 248. The spacecraft is not aimed at the star, and its instruments will have fallen silent long before.

source.title: NASA: Voyager’s interstellar mission

epsilon-eridani.name: Epsilon Eridani
epsilon-eridani.introduction: is a young orange dwarf about 10.5 light-years away in Eridanus, the third-closest star visible to the unaided eye. With a giant planet and belts of dusty debris, it looks like a younger version of our own Solar System.

sections.title: A younger Sun
sections.text: Most age estimates fall between 200 and 800 million years, a fraction of the Sun’s 4.6 billion. Like the young Sun, it is magnetically active, with overlapping activity cycles of about 3 and 13 years. Its stellar wind blows a bubble, or astrosphere, that would look wider than the full Moon from Earth.

sections.title: Listening for neighbors
sections.text: In 1960, Frank Drake’s Project Ozma pointed a radio telescope at Epsilon Eridani and Tau Ceti to listen for artificial signals. It was the first modern search for extraterrestrial intelligence; no signals were found.

sections.title: A Kuiper belt in the making
sections.text: Excess infrared light, first detected in 1983, revealed dust from collisions among comets and asteroids. The main belt lies about 70 AU from the star, comparable to our Kuiper belt early in its history. Webb imaging published in 2025 examined the warm dust closer in, near the giant planet’s orbit.

source.title: Wolff et al. 2025: Webb/MIRI imaging of the debris disk

sections.title: The giant planet Ægir
sections.text: Epsilon Eridani b, announced in 2000, circles the star every 7.3 years at about 3.5 AU. A 2025 study combining decades of Doppler measurements with Hipparcos, Hubble and Gaia astrometry weighed it at about one Jupiter mass, on a nearly circular orbit tilted like the outer dust belt. It has never been imaged directly; the picture above is an artist’s concept.

source.title: Thompson et al. 2025: Revised mass and orbit of Epsilon Eridani b

sections.title: Names from the sea
sections.text: In 2015 the IAU adopted Ran for the star and Ægir for its planet, the Norse sea goddess and her husband, as suggested by schoolchildren in Colbert, Washington. Science fiction had long favored the system: the Babylon 5 station and the planet Reach in the Halo games both orbit Epsilon Eridani.

lacaille-9352.name: Lacaille 9352
lacaille-9352.introduction: is one of the brightest red dwarfs in the sky, about 10.7 light-years away in Piscis Austrinus. Also known as Gliese 887, it has the fourth-highest proper motion of any known star and hosts a compact family of planets.

sections.title: Measured with precision
sections.text: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille recorded it during his survey of the southern sky in the 1750s, and Benjamin Gould noticed its rapid motion, about 6.9 arcseconds per year, in 1881. In 2001 it became the first red dwarf to have its angular diameter measured, revealing a star about 47% of the Sun’s width. A mismatch between Hipparcos and Gaia measurements of its motion hints at an unseen giant planet farther out.

sections.title: Four planets in a tight family
sections.text: Planets were first reported in 2020. A 2026 study combined new HARPS and ESPRESSO measurements, separated the star’s 39-day rotation signal, and reported four planets with years of about 4.4, 9.3, 21.8 and 50.8 days. The outermost, a super-Earth, lies in the modeled habitable zone. A fifth signal at 2.2 days remains a candidate. None of the planets transits, so their sizes are unknown.

source.title: Hartogh et al. 2026: RedDots study of GJ 887

ross-128.name: Ross 128
ross-128.introduction: is a red dwarf about 11 light-years away in Virgo, sometimes nicknamed Proxima Virginis. It hosts Ross 128 b, one of the nearest Earth-mass planets, and is unusually calm for a star of its type.

sections.title: A quiet host on its way here
sections.text: Many red dwarfs, Proxima Centauri among them, bombard their surroundings with flares. Ross 128 flares far less, which makes it the quietest nearby star known to host a temperate planet. It is moving toward us and is expected to become our nearest stellar neighbor in about 79,000 years.

source.title: ESO: A temperate world around a quiet star

sections.title: Ross 128 b
sections.text: Found with HARPS in 2017, the planet orbits every 9.9 days and has at least 1.4 times Earth’s mass. The starlight it receives could allow a temperate climate, but neither water nor an atmosphere has been detected. A 2024 reanalysis suggested a Mercury-like eccentric orbit, which would make its climate swing with every circuit.

source.title: Liebing et al. 2024: RedDots limits and Ross 128’s orbit

sections.title: The “weird signal” of 2017
sections.text: In spring 2017 the Arecibo radio telescope recorded unusual signals while observing Ross 128, briefly sparking speculation. Follow-up observations pointed to human-made interference: from Earth, the star appears in the same part of the sky as geostationary satellites.

ez-aquarii.name: EZ Aquarii
ez-aquarii.introduction: is a compact family of three red dwarfs about 11.1 light-years away in Aquarius, also called Gliese 866 or Luyten 789-6. Each of the three has only about a tenth of the Sun’s mass, close to the lower limit for a hydrogen-burning star.

sections.title: Three stars, two nested orbits
sections.text: A and C form a close pair with a nearly circular 3.8-day orbit, only about 0.03 AU apart: less than a tenth of Mercury’s distance from the Sun. B circles that pair every 823 days. Following both orbits gives precise masses, making the system a benchmark for weighing the smallest stars.

source.title: Ségransan et al. 2000: Accurate masses of low-mass stars

sections.title: Flares and spots
sections.text: William Kunkel identified it as a flare star in 1972 after observing seven flares. Rotating starspots cause smaller brightness changes as well. Its nearest stellar neighbor is Lacaille 9352.

cns5-gj-781.name: Wolf 1130
cns5-gj-781.introduction: is a triple system about 54 light-years away in Cygnus, also known as GJ 781, LHS 482 and the flare star V1513 Cygni. The red subdwarf A shares a tight orbit with B, an ultramassive white dwarf, while the cold brown dwarf C circles far outside the pair.

sections.title: A star circling a hidden heavyweight
sections.text: A and B orbit each other every 11.9 hours, only about 2.1 million kilometers apart: five and a half times the Moon’s distance from Earth. B has never been seen; it is too cool and faint to show up beside A. In 2018, astronomers weighed it through its pull on A, which swings toward and away from us at 121 km/s. B holds 1.24 times the Sun’s mass, the first ultramassive white dwarf found within 82 light-years of the Sun.

source.title: Mace et al. 2018: Wolf 1130, a triple with an ultramassive white dwarf

sections.title: A supernova in the making?
sections.text: The pair is slowly spiraling inward. Once they are about 1.1 solar radii apart, A will start spilling gas onto B, turning the system into a cataclysmic variable, a binary prone to sudden outbursts. B is already close to the 1.4-solar-mass limit that a white dwarf can support, so the added material could one day set off a Type Ia supernova.

source.title: Mace et al. 2018: Wolf 1130, a triple with an ultramassive white dwarf

sections.title: A brown dwarf in the far suburbs
sections.text: C was discovered in 2013 in images from NASA’s WISE infrared survey satellite. It is a metal-poor brown dwarf of type T8, only about 800 K (530 °C). At least 3,150 AU separate it from the inner pair, about 80 times Pluto’s distance from the Sun, yet it moves across the sky in step with them.

source.title: Mace et al. 2018: Wolf 1130, a triple with an ultramassive white dwarf

sections.title: A relic of the young Milky Way
sections.text: A has only about a fifth of the Sun’s share of iron, and its makeup and speed suggest the system is more than 10 billion years old, over twice the Sun’s age. B has had time to cool below 7,000 K and has been fading for at least 3.4 billion years. Its great mass points to a core of oxygen and neon rather than the usual carbon and oxygen.

source.title: Mace et al. 2018: Wolf 1130, a triple with an ultramassive white dwarf

sections.title: Caught on a photographic plate
sections.text: The name comes from Max Wolf, director of the Heidelberg-Königstuhl State Observatory, who photographed the sky to find faint stars that shift position from year to year. His catalog, first published in 1919, grew to more than 1,500 such stars; Wolf 359 is another. Wolf 1130 drifts 1.47 arcseconds a year, about 2 arcminutes in a human lifetime: roughly a sixteenth of the full Moon’s width.

source.title: Wikipedia: Max Wolf
